# Tallgrass kickoff

Graham Pruitt (owner), Leticia Navarro (dispatcher). At the shop on Kipling.

## How requests arrive today
- Email to service@tallgrass-home.com (Google Workspace).
- Website request form: WordPress + **Gravity Forms**. Fields: name, phone, address, service type, description,
  preferred day.
- Texts to the office line. Leticia reads them on the office phone. Moving the line to a Twilio number.

## Where they go
- Google Sheet **Dispatch Board**, one tab per day. Leticia assigns a tech in the "Tech" column and types a window.
- No ticket numbers today. Leticia finds jobs by customer name.

## Arrival windows
- 4-hour windows: morning 8-12, afternoon 12-4.
- Text the customer the window when a tech is assigned.

# Tallgrass on-call

On-call line: +13035550191. Twilio forwards calls and texts to whoever is on call that week. Emergency pages from
tallgrass-dispatch go to this line, never to a tech's own phone.

Rotation runs Monday 7:00 to the next Monday 7:00. From Leticia's sheet:

| Week of | On call |
|---|---|
| Sep 14 | Dmitri Kowal |
| Sep 21 | Ray Tanaka |
| Sep 28 | Carmen Ruiz |
| Oct 5 | Dmitri Kowal |

Swaps go through Leticia. She changes the forward in the Twilio console; nothing in the app needs to change.

# Tallgrass pilot, Sep 22-23

Two days of live requests with real customer texts. Leticia still watched the inboxes in case something slipped.

## Numbers
- 71 requests: 19 email, 22 web form, 30 text.
- All 71 ended up on the Dispatch Board. 6 were merged into an existing ticket (same phone within 30 minutes).
- 3 out of area, declined and put on the "Out of area" tab.
- Request to ticket: about 40 seconds on average. Leticia's retyping took about 25 minutes per request at busy times.
- 2 P1s (one burst pipe, one gas smell). Both paged the on-call line.

## Problems
- 4 customers never got their arrival text. Twilio error 30006: the number is a landline. Leticia had to call them.
- One customer replied "c" in lowercase. Worked fine.

## Next
- Check the line type before texting, and flag landline tickets for a phone call.

answer:
The one real problem in the Tallgrass pilot (Sep 22-23) was that 4 customers never got their arrival text. Twilio returned error 30006 because their numbers were landlines, so Leticia Navarro had to phone them.

The fix was tallgrass-dispatch PR #6, merged on 2026-09-25. Before the first text to a new number, it now checks the line type with Twilio Lookup and caches the result on the ticket. For landlines it sends no texts and sets the ticket's Contact column to `CALL CUSTOMER`, highlighted orange, so Leticia knows to call. Jules tested it against the 4 pilot numbers, and all 4 came back as landlines and were flagged.

The same PR also renamed the text sender to "Tallgrass Home Services". A customer who replied "c" in lowercase worked fine, so that wasn't a problem.

# Tallgrass kickoff

Graham Pruitt (owner), Leticia Navarro (dispatcher). At the shop on Kipling.

## How requests arrive today
- Email to service@tallgrass-home.com (Google Workspace).
- Website request form: WordPress + **Gravity Forms**. Fields: name, phone, address, service type, description,
  preferred day.
- Texts to the office line. Leticia reads them on the office phone. Moving the line to a Twilio number.

## Where they go
- Google Sheet **Dispatch Board**, one tab per day. Leticia assigns a tech in the "Tech" column and types a window.
- No ticket numbers today. Leticia finds jobs by customer name.

## Arrival windows
- 4-hour windows: morning 8-12, afternoon 12-4.
- Text the customer the window when a tech is assigned.
[2026-09-01 gmail] Help with service requests From: Graham Pruitt <graham@tallgrass-home.com> To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev> Date: 2026-09-01T12:42:46Z Hi Jules, I heard you talk at the Wheat Ridge Business Association breakfast in August about automating the boring stuff, and I've got some boring stuff. I own Tallgrass Home Services in Wheat Ridge. Heating, cooling and plumbing, 12 technicians (8 HVAC, 4 plumbers). Service requests come in three ways: email to service@, the request form on our website, and texts to our office line. Leticia, our dispatcher, retypes every one of them into our dispatch spreadsheet. That's about 3 hours of her day. We get around 40 requests a day this time of year and up to 90 on a cold snap. The other half of the problem: customers call all day asking when the tech is coming. I'd like them to get a text with the arrival window as soon as we assign someone. Can we talk this week? Mornings are best, we start at 6:30. Graham Pruitt Owner, Tallgrass Home Services (303) 555-0163

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 213

Hi,

Every automation fails eventually. The ones that hurt are the ones that fail quietly. This week: how to find out before your customers do.

1. A HEARTBEAT, NOT A HOPE

If a job should run every hour, have it write a timestamp somewhere (a cell, a file, a tiny status page). Then have a second, separate check that complains when the timestamp is more than two hours old. The second check is the one that saves you, because a dead job cannot report its own death.

2. A DEAD-LETTER TAB

When a row cannot be processed, do not skip it and do not crash. Move it to a tab called "needs a human" with the error message beside it. A florist we spoke to lost six orders over a month because her script quietly dropped any row with a blank delivery field. A dead-letter tab would have shown all six on day one.

3. MAKE REPLAYS SAFE

# Tallgrass pilot, Sep 22-23

Two days of live requests with real customer texts. Leticia still watched the inboxes in case something slipped.

## Numbers
- 71 requests: 19 email, 22 web form, 30 text.
- All 71 ended up on the Dispatch Board. 6 were merged into an existing ticket (same phone within 30 minutes).
- 3 out of area, declined and put on the "Out of area" tab.
- Request to ticket: about 40 seconds on average. Leticia's retyping took about 25 minutes per request at busy times.
- 2 P1s (one burst pipe, one gas smell). Both paged the on-call line.

## Problems
- 4 customers never got their arrival text. Twilio error 30006: the number is a landline. Leticia had to call them.
- One customer replied "c" in lowercase. Worked fine.

## Next
- Check the line type before texting, and flag landline tickets for a phone call.

# Tallgrass pilot, Sep 22-23

Two days of live requests with real customer texts. Leticia still watched the inboxes in case something slipped.

## Numbers
- 71 requests: 19 email, 22 web form, 30 text.
- All 71 ended up on the Dispatch Board. 6 were merged into an existing ticket (same phone within 30 minutes).
- 3 out of area, declined and put on the "Out of area" tab.
- Request to ticket: about 40 seconds on average. Leticia's retyping took about 25 minutes per request at busy times.
- 2 P1s (one burst pipe, one gas smell). Both paged the on-call line.

## Problems
- 4 customers never got their arrival text. Twilio error 30006: the number is a landline. Leticia had to call them.
- One customer replied "c" in lowercase. Worked fine.

## Next
- Check the line type before texting, and flag landline tickets for a phone call.
answer: The system shouldn't create two tickets for one problem. In the Sep 22-23 pilot, a new request with the same phone number as an existing ticket, within 30 minutes, was merged into that ticket, and 6 of the 71 requests were merged this way. My records don't say how an email is matched to a phone number when it has none, so I can't say how that case works.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that a message with the same phone number as a ticket opened within the last 30 minutes is merged into that ticket rather than creating a new one, and its caveat does not contradict the reference.

question: How often does tallgrass-dispatch check the service@ inbox?
gold: Every 2 minutes, through the Gmail API; processed mail gets the Ticketed label.

input.query: Tallgrass customer replies R reschedule arrival text

answer:
The arrival text ends with "Reply C to confirm or R to reschedule."

- **C:** The ticket is marked confirmed.
- **R:** A "Call back to reschedule" note is added to the ticket, and the ticket is highlighted yellow for Leticia so she can phone the customer.

Landline customers get no texts at all. Their ticket is flagged `CALL CUSTOMER` in orange, and Leticia phones them with the window instead.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that C confirms the ticket and R adds a call-back-to-reschedule note and highlights the ticket yellow for Leticia, with no contradictions to the reference.

question: Why did some Tallgrass customers get 'arriving today' texts the night before?
gold: The code used UTC dates (datetime.utcnow), so after 18:00 in Denver tomorrow's jobs read as today. Fixed to use America/Denver and name the weekday.

input.query: Tallgrass arriving today texts sent the night before
Tallgrass pilot timezone reminder send window bug

answer:
The records say the arrival-text bug came from `render_window()` in tallgrass-dispatch. It chose "today" or "tomorrow" using `datetime.utcnow().date()`, which is the UTC date, not the Denver date.

From that, my inference is that after about 6 pm Denver time (UTC midnight in September) the function already saw the next day. A text sent that evening for a job the following day would then say "arriving today". The records don't include the fix or the exact affected customers, so that part is inferred from the cause.
judge_reason: The answer correctly explains the UTC date rollover but contradicts the reference by saying the records lack a fix, which was to use America/Denver and name the weekday.

# Tallgrass pilot, Sep 22-23

Two days of live requests with real customer texts. Leticia still watched the inboxes in case something slipped.

## Numbers
- 71 requests: 19 email, 22 web form, 30 text.
- All 71 ended up on the Dispatch Board. 6 were merged into an existing ticket (same phone within 30 minutes).
- 3 out of area, declined and put on the "Out of area" tab.
- Request to ticket: about 40 seconds on average. Leticia's retyping took about 25 minutes per request at busy times.
- 2 P1s (one burst pipe, one gas smell). Both paged the on-call line.

## Problems
- 4 customers never got their arrival text. Twilio error 30006: the number is a landline. Leticia had to call them.
- One customer replied "c" in lowercase. Worked fine.

## Next
- Check the line type before texting, and flag landline tickets for a phone call.

In kindling-waitlist, open_spot in app/offers.py picks the next waitlisted member who has not had an offer for that spot, texts them, and sets expires_at to sent_at plus CLAIM_WINDOW.
The shorter 15-minute Kindling waitlist claim window is meant to let more waitlisted people respond before last call when a late-afternoon spot opens.

input.query: kindling-waitlist parse_reply accepted variants YES Y Yes!

answer: As of the 2026-09-26 fix, a reply claims a spot if its first word is yes, y, yep, yeah, or ya. Case and punctuation are ignored, so "Yes!", "y", "yep", and "Yeah I'll take it" all work, while "no" and "maybe" don't. Before that fix, only an exact "YES" worked, which is why Marco's "y" and Bea's "Yes!" failed in the 2026-09-25 staff test. One of the profile notes still says "y" doesn't claim a spot. That note is from 2026-09-25 and the fix is newer, so I'm treating it as out of date.

# Alder & Finch discovery

Callie Brennan (ops manager, day-to-day contact), Gideon Pratt (owner, approves budget), Manny Esquivel

- ~25-40 requests a week. Text, email, phone. NightDesk answering service after hours.

- Mon-Fri **8:00-17:00**, Denver time. Office closed on federal holidays.

Jules Marlow
Marlow Works

From: Quiet Workflow <weekly@quietworkflow.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-02T12:30:05Z

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 212 | Automation for small teams without an IT department

Hi,

Four people wrote in this week with the same question: "Orders come in from three places and I type them into a spreadsheet. Now what?" So let's walk through it.

THREE WAYS ORDERS REACH A SPREADSHEET

1. A form that writes to Google Sheets. Boring, reliable, and the right answer more often than people want to admit. If you can send customers to a form, do that first.

2. Email parsing. Forward order emails to a mailbox a script reads, pull out the fields, append a row. Works when the senders are other businesses writing in a consistent template. Falls apart with humans.
[2026-09-09 gmail] Quiet Workflow 213: When the automation breaks at 2 a.m.
From: Quiet Workflow <weekly@quietworkflow.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-09T12:30:01Z

QUIET WORKFLOW
Issue 213

Hi,

Every automation fails eventually. The ones that hurt are the ones that fail quietly. This week: how to find out before your customers do.

1. A HEARTBEAT, NOT A HOPE

If a job should run every hour, have it write a timestamp somewhere (a cell, a file, a tiny status page). Then have a second, separate check that complains when the timestamp is more than two hours old. The second check is the one that saves you, because a dead job cannot report its own death.

2. A DEAD-LETTER TAB

When a row cannot be processed, do not skip it and do not crash. Move it to a tab called "needs a human" with the error message beside it. A florist we spoke to lost six orders over a month because her script quietly dropped any row with a blank delivery field. A dead-letter tab would have shown all six on day one.

3. MAKE REPLAYS SAFE

answer:
An email to repairs@alderfinchpm.com is forwarded to Postmark inbound. Intake lowercases the sender's address and looks it up in the email column of the nightly Buildium roster. If it matches, it opens a work order for that unit, copies any photos, and replies to the sender with the work order number.

If the sender isn't on the roster, as decided in alderfinch-dispatch issue #4 on 2026-09-17 (Callie agreed), no work order opens and no auto-reply goes out. The email goes to the "Unmatched" queue at /dashboard/unmatched on Manny's dashboard. He checks it each morning and after lunch, and either links it to a unit (which opens the work order and sends the normal reply) or dismisses it. This replaces the earlier behavior of opening a unit-less work order.

answer:
At Alder & Finch, these after-hours requests page the on-call tech:
- an active leak or flooding
- a gas smell (the tenant is told to leave and call 911 first, then the page goes out)
- a sewage backup
- no power to the whole unit
- an exterior door or window that won't lock
- no heat, but only from October 1 through April 30, so it counts as an emergency starting today

If the tech doesn't press 1 within 10 minutes, the page goes to Manny, then to Gideon after another 10 minutes, and then it starts over. Lockouts aren't emergencies, so the tenant gets Lockhart's number and the $95 fee. Everything else gets an auto-reply and waits until 8:00 the next business day.

# Alder & Finch discovery

Callie Brennan (ops manager, day-to-day contact), Gideon Pratt (owner, approves budget), Manny Esquivel
(maintenance coordinator, on-call boss).

## Today
- ~25-40 requests a week. Text, email, phone. NightDesk answering service after hours.
- Tenant roster lives in **Buildium**. Callie can schedule a nightly tenant export (CSV) to an SFTP folder.
  Columns: unit, building, tenant name, mobile, email, lang, lease end.
- `lang` is `en` or `es`. About 30% of households prefer Spanish.

## Business hours
- Mon-Fri **8:00-17:00**, Denver time. Office closed on federal holidays.
- Outside business hours = after hours.
## After-hours emergencies (page the on-call tech)
- Active water leak or flooding
- No heat, **October 1 to April 30 only** (in summer it waits for morning)
- Smell of gas
- Sewage backup
- No power to the whole unit
- Exterior door or window that won't lock

Gas: the reply tells the tenant to leave the unit and call 911 first. We page the on-call tech after that, we don't
send them in first.

Lockouts are **not** emergencies. After hours the tenant gets Lockhart Lock & Key's number and pays the
**$95** after-hours lockout fee directly.

Everything else after hours: auto-reply, handle next business day.

## On-call escalation
- Page the on-call tech (phone call, not just a text). If no answer in **15 minutes**, call Manny.
- Manny: "15 is already long when water's coming through a ceiling." Gideon was fine with 15 for now.

## Vendors
- Vendors can do up to **$500** of work without asking. Over that, Manny approves first.
- Vendor list: Callie will send it (in the client folder).

## Timeline
- Gideon wants it live in all 7 buildings on **October 1**.

# Bluestem discovery call

Lena Okafor (volunteer coordinator), Marcus Pell (executive director).

## Who decides
- Marcus Pell approves spending. Anything over **$5,000** also needs a board vote. Board meets Sep 29.

## Money
- Paid from a **$10,000 technology grant** from the Front Range Neighbors Fund. Has to be spent by **December 31**.

## What they want
- Volunteers pick shifts from their phone. No accounts, no app to install. A link and their phone number.
- One reminder text the evening before a shift, around 6pm.
- Each garden lead sees who's coming to their garden that week.
- All 9 gardens at once.
- Texts in **English and Spanish**. About a third of volunteers prefer Spanish.
- Volunteers **under 16** have to have a parent or guardian signed up for the **same shift**. Today Lena checks
  this by eye in the sheet.

# Bluestem discovery call

Lena Okafor (volunteer coordinator), Marcus Pell (executive director).

## Who decides
- Marcus Pell approves spending. Anything over **$5,000** also needs a board vote. Board meets Sep 29.

## Money
- Paid from a **$10,000 technology grant** from the Front Range Neighbors Fund. Has to be spent by **December 31**.

## What they want
- Volunteers pick shifts from their phone. No accounts, no app to install. A link and their phone number.
- One reminder text the evening before a shift, around 6pm.
- Each garden lead sees who's coming to their garden that week.
- All 9 gardens at once.
- Texts in **English and Spanish**. About a third of volunteers prefer Spanish.
- Volunteers **under 16** have to have a parent or guardian signed up for the **same shift**. Today Lena checks
  this by eye in the sheet.

# Bluestem discovery call

Lena Okafor (volunteer coordinator), Marcus Pell (executive director).

## Who decides
- Marcus Pell approves spending. Anything over **$5,000** also needs a board vote. Board meets Sep 29.

## Money
- Paid from a **$10,000 technology grant** from the Front Range Neighbors Fund. Has to be spent by **December 31**.

## What they want
- Volunteers pick shifts from their phone. No accounts, no app to install. A link and their phone number.
- One reminder text the evening before a shift, around 6pm.
- Each garden lead sees who's coming to their garden that week.
- All 9 gardens at once.
- Texts in **English and Spanish**. About a third of volunteers prefer Spanish.

Lena Okafor (volunteer coordinator), Marcus Pell (executive director).

# Bluestem discovery call

Lena Okafor (volunteer coordinator), Marcus Pell (executive director).

## Who decides
- Marcus Pell approves spending. Anything over **$5,000** also needs a board vote. Board meets Sep 29.

## Money
- Paid from a **$10,000 technology grant** from the Front Range Neighbors Fund. Has to be spent by **December 31**.

## What they want
- Volunteers pick shifts from their phone. No accounts, no app to install. A link and their phone number.
- One reminder text the evening before a shift, around 6pm.
- Each garden lead sees who's coming to their garden that week.
- All 9 gardens at once.
- Texts in **English and Spanish**. About a third of volunteers prefer Spanish.
- Volunteers **under 16** have to have a parent or guardian signed up for the **same shift**. Today Lena checks
  this by eye in the sheet.
answer: No. The board changed the rollout. It starts with three pilot gardens (Larkspur, Tenth Avenue and Mill Creek), and the other six join in the spring after the pilot has been tested. Lena had originally asked for all 9 at once, but the price ($9,600) and the November 16 date stay the same.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that the original nine-garden rollout was reduced to three named pilot gardens, with the remaining six joining in spring after the pilot is tested, and its extra details do not contradict the reference.

question: How do I replay an old Stripe event without it failing the timestamp check?
gold: Pass the endpoint secret: `hookbox replay <id> --to ... --stripe-secret whsec_...` re-signs the event with the current time, so it passes Stripe's 5-minute tolerance.

## Related memories
hookbox replay has a --stripe-secret option that re-signs a Stripe event with the current timestamp before replaying it.
Stripe signatures include a timestamp, and Stripe libraries reject signatures older than 5 minutes by default, so forwarding headers alone does not make old replayed events verify.
Because --stripe-secret re-signs with the current timestamp, replayed Stripe events older than Stripe's 5 minute tolerance still pass signature verification.
In issue #41, replaying a Stripe event with hookbox replay returned HTTP 400 from the Flask app with "No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload", while the original Stripe delivery had passed.
The hookbox test tests/test_replay_stripe.py records a signed event, replays it with --stripe-secret one hour later using a frozen clock, and verifies it with stripe.Webhook.construct_event.

answer:
Use `hookbox replay` with the `--stripe-secret` option, which was added in hookbox 0.8.1. For example: `hookbox replay 118 --to http://localhost:5000/stripe/webhook --stripe-secret whsec_...`. The option re-signs the event with the current timestamp using your endpoint secret, so events older than Stripe's 5-minute tolerance still pass verification.

Forwarding the recorded headers alone isn't enough, because the original signature's timestamp is what gets rejected.

question: Why were replayed Stripe events failing in hookbox?
gold: Replay forwarded only Content-Type and User-Agent, so the Stripe-Signature header was dropped. It now forwards every recorded header except Host, Content-Length and the hop-by-hop headers Connection, Transfer-Encoding and Keep-Alive (fixed in 0.8.1).

answer:
Replayed Stripe events failed because `hookbox replay` only forwarded the `Content-Type` and `User-Agent` headers. That meant the `Stripe-Signature` header was dropped, so the Flask app returned a 400 ("No signatures found matching the expected signature"). The allowlist dated from 0.3, when only JSON bodies mattered.

A second problem was that Stripe's signature includes a timestamp, and libraries reject anything older than 5 minutes by default. The fix in 0.8.1 (issue #41) forwards all recorded headers except `Host`, `Content-Length` and hop-by-hop ones. It also adds `--stripe-secret`, which re-signs the event with the current time so old events pass verification.

## Related memories
Jules wants the hookbox database file to actually shrink after pruning.
hookbox databases created before version 0.9.0 do not shrink after pruning until they have been vacuumed once.
On a copy of a 612 MB hookbox test database, running hookbox vacuum and then a 14-day prune on 2026-09-15 removed 418,233 events and shrank the file to 41 MB.
hookbox sets PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL for newly created databases and runs PRAGMA incremental_vacuum after each prune.
hookbox has a maybe-for-1.0 idea to split the database per source.
## Docs
- `prune(db, keep_days, now)` runs `delete from events where pinned = 0 and received_at < ?`. `keep_days == 0` returns early.
- `serve` calls `prune` at startup and from a background task every hour.

On shrinking the file: SQLite doesn't give pages back to the OS after a delete unless the database uses `auto_vacuum`. I'll set `PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL` for new databases and run `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum` after each prune. The catch is that `auto_vacuum` can only change on an existing database through a full `VACUUM`, so databases created before 0.9.0 won't shrink until they're vacuumed once. I'll add `hookbox vacuum` for that and say so in the changelog.

## Docs
## If the network fails
Venue wifi is a guest network, so tunnels may not work. Backup: everyone loads the recorded events offline with
`hookbox load fixtures/workshop.jsonl` (12 Stripe events, two of them deliberately malformed) and does both
exercises from there. Put the command on the handout.
A florist we spoke to lost six orders over a month because her script quietly dropped any row with a blank delivery field. A dead-letter tab would have shown all six on day one.

3. MAKE REPLAYS SAFE

Sooner or later you will run the same batch twice. Give every record a stable ID (order number plus source, for example) and check for it before you write. If running the job twice gives the same result as running it once, you can retry without fear.

4. ONE LOUD ALERT BEATS TEN QUIET ONES

Alert fatigue is real. Pick one channel (a text, a Slack message to yourself), send only failures, and include what failed and what to do. "Order sync failed: 3 rows in needs-a-human, see sheet" is useful. "Error 500" is not.

READER CORNER

Rosalind from a bike repair shop in Ohio shared her checklist for new automations: who gets told when it fails, where the raw input lives, how to turn it off. Three lines. We printed it. https://quietworkflow.example/community/three-line-checklist

Tobias

hookbox replay has a --stripe-secret option that re-signs a Stripe event with the current timestamp before replaying it.
In issue #41, replaying a Stripe event with hookbox replay returned HTTP 400 from the Flask app with "No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload", while the original Stripe delivery had passed.

you are ready or not. If you plan to take pre-orders for pies, rolls and centerpiece cakes, the decisions you make now determine whether the week before is joyful or a scramble.

DECIDE THREE THINGS

1. How many can you actually bake? Count oven racks, not hope. Set a cap per item per day and refuse to sell past it.
2. When do pre-orders close? Practices vary. Rye Street closes the Sunday before. A Portland shop closes eight days ahead for pies and three for rolls, because rolls are simpler. The point is to write it down and say it everywhere.
3. How do people order? Online forms, a phone line, in person, and now text messages. Several shops told us texting is how regulars prefer to order, and it is also the least structured. THE RECALL LETTER
Issue 79

AFTER THE MISSED VISIT: WHAT PATIENTS ARE TOLD, AND WHAT WORKS

Most offices have a reminder process. Far fewer have a process for what happens after the patient does not show up. This issue is about that gap.

THE SAME-DAY FOLLOW-UP

Four practices we spoke to send a short note within two hours of a missed visit: "We missed you today. Want to find a new time? Reply here or call us." Rebooking within 14 days was roughly twice as likely as in offices that did nothing. The tone matters. Notes that mentioned a fee in the first line were answered less than half as often.

THE WAITLIST

A waitlist only works if it is short and current. Practices that texted a waitlist of five to ten people, first reply wins, filled about one in three same-day openings. Practices with a list of 80 people filled almost none, because half the numbers were stale.

**Added to `git/.config/git/config`.** `git st` is `status -sb`. `git lg` is a one-line graph log with relative dates, authors and refs. `git cleanup` deletes local branches already merged into `main`.

**How `cleanup` stays safe.** It lists branches with `--merged main`, skips `main` and the current branch, and deletes with `-d`, so git refuses anything unmerged even if the filter were wrong.

**Checked.** I ran it on a scratch repository with a merged branch, an unmerged branch, the current branch and `main`. Only the merged one was deleted, and a second run with nothing to delete exited cleanly. The pager shows the colors because `LESS` contains `-R`. It only looks at local branches, so branches that were squash-merged on GitHub show as unmerged and stay until you remove them by hand.
answer: Run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. It moves the branch back one commit and leaves the changes staged. `git reset HEAD~1` (the default `--mixed`) would unstage them but keep them in your working tree. If you've already pushed the commit, undoing it means rewriting history, so `git revert HEAD` is safer.

answer:
Group by the email and keep the ones that appear more than once:

```sql
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

To catch case or whitespace variants, group by `LOWER(TRIM(email))` instead. To see the full duplicate rows, join that result back to `users` on the email. I'm assuming the table is called `users` and the column is `email`.

answer: HTTP 304 means "Not Modified." The server is telling the client that the resource hasn't changed since the version it has cached. This usually happens after a conditional request with `If-None-Match` (ETag) or `If-Modified-Since`. The server sends no body, and the client reuses its cached copy.

**Added to `git/.config/git/config`.** `git st` is `status -sb`. `git lg` is a one-line graph log with relative dates, authors and refs. `git cleanup` deletes local branches already merged into `main`.

**How `cleanup` stays safe.** It lists branches with `--merged main`, skips `main` and the current branch, and deletes with `-d`, so git refuses anything unmerged even if the filter were wrong.

**Checked.** I ran it on a scratch repository with a merged branch, an unmerged branch, the current branch and `main`. Only the merged one was deleted, and a second run with nothing to delete exited cleanly. The pager shows the colors because `LESS` contains `-R`. It only looks at local branches, so branches that were squash-merged on GitHub show as unmerged and stay until you remove them by hand.

HOW TO SAY YES TO THE COFFEE SHOP

A neighborhood cafe asks if you can supply them with croissants, muffins and a sourdough loaf. The answer is usually yes. The question is how to say yes without wrecking your retail day.

START WITH A STANDING ORDER

A standing order (the same items on the same days) is easier to produce than one-off requests and easier to forecast. Ask for a small commitment: three days a week, set quantities, with changes by a certain time the day before.

KNOW YOUR PAR LEVELS

Ask the cafe what they sell on a normal day. Then ask for their par, the number they want on the shelf at open. Bake to the par, not to the average. Bakeries that skipped this step got angry calls the first Saturday.

answer: `shopt -s nullglob` makes a glob that matches no files expand to nothing. Without it, bash leaves the literal pattern in place, so `for f in *.txt` with no `.txt` files runs once with `f` set to the string `*.txt`. With it, the loop body never runs, and `files=(*.txt)` gives an empty array. It applies to the whole shell until you turn it off with `shopt -u nullglob`. It also works on macOS's bash 3.2, so it's safe in your dotfiles' `install.sh`.

answer: `===` is the strict equality operator. It compares both value and type, with no type coercion. `==` is the loose operator. It converts the operands to a common type before comparing, which gives surprising results like `0 == ""`, `"1" == 1`, `null == undefined` and `[] == false`, all of which are true. Using `===` keeps comparisons predictable and avoids those coercion bugs. The usual exception is `x == null`, which deliberately matches both `null` and `undefined`.

From: The Backhaul <desk@backhaulbrief.example>
To: Jules Marlow <jules@marlowworks.dev>
Date: 2026-09-11T12:00:11Z

THE BACKHAUL
Vol. 9, No. 34

FREIGHT AUDIT SEASON: WHERE INVOICE ERRORS HIDE

With fourth-quarter budgets being set, shippers are taking a harder look at what they paid carriers in the first three quarters. Auditors we spoke to say a typical mid-size shipper overpays between one and three percent on freight invoices, mostly through errors that are tedious rather than clever.

The top five, in the order auditors say they find them:

1. Duplicate invoices, usually the same load billed once by the carrier and again after a rebill.
2. Accessorial charges (liftgate, residential delivery, detention) with no supporting proof of delivery.
3. Fuel surcharge calculated on the wrong index week.
4. Rate drift, where the invoiced linehaul does not match the contracted lane rate.
5. Weight or class corrections applied after the fact with no reweigh ticket.

THE DOCUMENT PROBLEM
to 30, 31 plus. The goal is not shame. It is to see whether the late ones belong to one client (a process problem on their side) or to many (a process problem on yours).

3. CHECK YOUR CONCENTRATION

If one client is more than 40 percent of the quarter's revenue, write that number down and look at it again next quarter. No need to panic. You just want it to be a decision, not a surprise.

4. PAY YOURSELF ON PURPOSE

Move money from the business account to your personal account on a fixed day with a fixed rule, even if the rule is "whatever is left after the buffer." Irregular income gets easier when the transfer is boring.

5. WRITE DOWN ONE CHANGE

Only one. Last quarter's change for the editor was "invoice on acceptance, not on delivery." It moved her average payment day by about nine days.

LINKS
Day 14:
"Hi Jordan, invoice 1043 is two weeks past due. Can you tell me the date it will be paid? I will pause new work until I have a date."

Notice the pattern. Each message names the invoice, names one next step, and offers a way out that is not a confrontation. Readers who switched to this sequence told us roughly a third of their "late" invoices were paid within a day of the first message.

2. READER QUESTION

"One client pays all vendors in a single batch on the 20th. Should I time my invoices to land just before it?"

Yes. Ask their accounts payable contact for the batch calendar once, then put the cutoff in your own calendar. A twelve-minute email now saves a month of waiting every time you miss the window by a day.

3. WORTH YOUR TIME

answer: Set `Content-Type: application/json`. With curl, that's `curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"a":1}' URL`. # Pricing thoughts

No numbers here, just ways of thinking.

## Value pricing, in general
- Price follows what the outcome is worth to the buyer, not hours spent.
- A tool that saves a small team a few hours of repetitive work every week has a value that has little to do with how long it took to write.
- The hardest part is learning what the problem costs them now. Ask.

## Questions to ask
- What happens if nothing changes?
- Who feels the pain: the owner, the manager, or the person doing the clicking?
- What would "done" look like in one sentence?

## Things to be careful about
- Fixed fees punish scope creep unless scope is written down.
- Hourly rewards slow work.
- Discounts teach buyers to ask for them. Trading scope is cleaner.
